aAbout: Argos Atlas is a hosted real-time world map that aggregates already-open official feeds — above all public cameras, which it claims number over 200,000 from official portals in more than 190 countries — and paints everything that moves around them on one flat map: flights, ships, war frontlines, verified events, infrastructure, earthquakes, fires and prediction markets. The live map is free with a free account; ARGOS PRO adds recording, history, an AI analyst layer and a 3D globe mode. Its maker is not named on its official pages.
aStrengths: Argos Atlas is the deeper working atlas: an order of magnitude more cameras (its claim), camera recording with a 24-hour scrubbable archive, flight and ship history (7–90 days), sanctions and dark-vessel flags, verified frontlines and events, geofence alerts and a 16-camera videowall. It asks nothing of your computer — a free account in any browser — and its team plans aim it at newsrooms and analysts, not just the curious.
bAbout: EarthCam runs a network of live webcams anchored by famous places — Times Square in New York is the signature view — organised into destination pages and EarthCam TV channels that package cameras into themed streams. Alongside the free consumer network it sells professional construction-camera systems to businesses, with managed hardware, archiving and time-lapse. Many public cameras are watchable free in the browser and in its mobile apps, with weather information shown alongside some cameras, and no account is needed to watch.
bStrengths: EarthCam is the deeper platform for famous places: a large, long-running network of scenic and tourist cameras anchored by Times Square, curated viewing through EarthCam TV, and professional construction-camera services with managed hardware, archiving and time-lapse for commercial clients. For watching a specific famous place — or for a business that needs a camera installed and managed — EarthCam's camera-specific depth and history beat a generalist atlas.
betterAnswer: They solve different problems. EarthCam is a dedicated webcam portal built around famous places — open it and watch, no account, no install — with a professional construction-camera business alongside. Argos Atlas is a hosted multi-layer atlas built around camera scale (200,000+ claimed) plus flight and ship tracking, recording, history and verification layers, free to open with an account and paid to remember. If you want to *watch a place*, open EarthCam; if you want to *monitor the world around the cameras* from any browser, open Argos Atlas.

verdictA: Choose Argos Atlas if you want a ready-to-open working map with the biggest claimed camera catalogue, flights and ships around the cameras, recording, history and alerts — and you're willing to create an account and pay for the memory features.
verdictB: Choose EarthCam if you want to watch famous places right now with no account — Times Square and other landmark cameras, TV-style curated channels — or if you need professional construction-camera services for a business site.
verdictLine: Argos Atlas is the workhorse — a hosted camera-first atlas that tracks and records what it sees. EarthCam is the destination — a curated network of famous views you can open instantly, plus a professional camera business. One is a free website with paid memory behind an account; the other is free viewing with no account at all.
worldEye: If Argos's account wall and ads are the friction there, and EarthCam's camera-only view feels narrow, WorldEye is the middle path: a hosted 3D globe that opens free in any browser with no signup at all — 74,229 public cameras across 105 countries, live flights, ships, satellites, weather, earthquakes and wildfires in the same view. It doesn't record cameras like Argos or run managed construction cameras like EarthCam, and its Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) buys an OSINT toolkit and intel feeds rather than camera archives.
